title: The Guerrilla-War-of-the-Mind Strategy: Do Not Fight the Last War
hook: The old sales deck feels safe because it once worked, which is exactly why it can betray you now.
counterintuition: Experience can become a costume. Read the present first, then decide which parts of the old playbook still fit.
tryThisNow: Draw two columns: what actually changed, and what merely sounds new. Circle the first old tactic that no longer fits the live terrain.
keyTakeaway: Past success should be evidence, not command; inspect the current terrain before memory turns a former advantage into today's blind spot.

breakdown.fastRead:
"This deck got us our first fifty clients," Sophie says, tapping the old slides before the municipal bid review. That is the problem. The private homeowners who once bought on speed and charm are gone. City procurement wants compliance records, insurance detail, and proof the crews can work around schools.

Fighting the last war means letting an old victory choose for a new situation. The cure is present-tense reading. What is actually in front of you? What only resembles the past? What condition has changed enough that yesterday's strength now creates risk?

Do not worship novelty either. Some problems wear new language and still obey old rules. Read first. Then choose.
breakdown.deepRead:
Sophie can feel the old confidence arrive before the meeting starts. Her solar company grew by moving fast, answering calls the same day, and closing homeowners before competitors found the roof. Now the company is bidding on municipal buildings, and she is about to lead with the same speed story. The procurement checklist on the table is telling her the terrain has changed.

Memory is trying to run the meeting.

A previous win is useful only after it has been tested against current facts. In the old market, speed signaled competence because homeowners wanted relief from a confusing purchase. In the municipal market, speed without documentation signals risk. The same behavior changes meaning when the buyer, rules, stakes, and downside change.

Sophie stops the deck on slide three. She writes three live constraints on the whiteboard: public insurance exposure, work near occupied schools, published scoring criteria. Then she cuts the homeowner testimonials and moves the safety record to the front. She is not throwing away experience. She is refusing to let experience give orders before the room has been read.

The reversal matters. Grace faces a magazine membership launch and keeps hearing that everything is different because subscriptions are digital now. But readers still renew when the work feels scarce, useful, and trustworthy. The interface changed. The underlying promise did not. Present-tense reading protects you from stale habits and from novelty theater.
breakdown.fullRead:
Rachel is on the sideline of a youth soccer academy practice when the new league schedule arrives. The coaches around her keep talking about last year's tournament run. Press early, win the ball high, wear teams down by halftime. It worked beautifully in the old league, where the academy was bigger, fitter, and deeper than almost every opponent.

The new league is different. Two opponents have technical midfielders who invite pressure and pass through it. Travel weekends are longer. Referees call contact tighter. The academy's old advantage may still matter, but it cannot be allowed to answer every question before the new facts speak.

This is how the last war gets into the mind. It does not announce itself as laziness. It arrives as confidence, craft, and proof. It says, we have seen this before. It points to the trophy photo on the office wall. It makes adjustment feel like betrayal of what made you good. That is why past success can be more dangerous than failure. Failure usually asks for review. Success asks for repetition.

You need a small discipline at the front of any changed situation: separate resemblance from reality. A new problem may remind you of an old one because both involve a buyer, a deadline, a rival, or a public decision. That resemblance is not enough. Ask what has changed in incentives, rules, timing, information, risk, and power. Ask what stayed stable. Only then should the old playbook be allowed back into the room.

Laura learns this in a craft brewery's move into grocery distribution. Her taproom launch playbook was intimacy: know the regulars, make the brewer visible, sell the story of the batch. Grocery buyers care about shelf velocity, delivery reliability, and margin protection. When she leads with the taproom story, the buyer smiles and asks for sell-through data. Laura sees the mistake. She is answering a retail channel with a neighborhood script.

The answer is not to become allergic to the past. The past contains tools, scars, and judgment you paid for. Sophie's discipline is not blank-slate thinking. Rachel should not erase what pressing taught her team about energy and risk. Laura should not pretend her brand story has no value. The move is sequencing: read the present first, then decide which old tools still earn their place.

The novelty trap sits on the other side. Anna works in university admissions when AI-written essays become the panic of the season. Some colleagues want to discard every old reading practice because the file now feels contaminated by a new technology. Anna slows the room down. They still need evidence of fit, curiosity, judgment, and actual work. The essays are less reliable, so interviews, graded writing samples, and teacher context matter more. The aim did not change. The evidence mix did.

That distinction saves judgment. If everything new demands a new doctrine, you become easy prey for fashion. If every new condition is forced into an old frame, you become predictable and brittle. The mind has to move like a guerrilla here: light enough to leave the old fort, disciplined enough not to run toward every shiny flag.

James sees the same pattern after a breach report crosses the cybersecurity team's dashboard. The intrusion resembles the phishing wave they handled last quarter, and the incident lead reaches for the same containment checklist. Then James notices the customer call transcript: users did not click a fake login link. They approved a real device prompt after a phone call from someone who already knew internal project names. The old checklist would close the wrong door.

The live terrain gets the first vote. Memory can advise after that.

At 6:30 p.m., the newsroom wants to reuse the advertising pitch that once sold print pages to local shops. Grace writes two lines on the proof: readers pay for trust, sponsors paid for reach. Before launch copy locks, she needs to decide which old promise still carries.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the trust promise and drop the sponsor-reach pitch. Build the membership offer around scarce reporting, reader access, and clear value rather than ad-era language.
examples.whyItMatters: The product changed from audience attention to reader commitment. Grace should not toss out the magazine's reputation, but the old buyer logic no longer fits.

Before, James would run the phishing playbook: reset passwords, block domains, warn users. After reading the transcript, he sees callers used real project names to trigger device approvals. questions.prompt: A founder keeps using the launch tactics that worked for early adopters, even though enterprise buyers now ask first about procurement, security, and support. What is the core problem?
choices: She is letting a prior victory define a changed situation.
She is refusing to respect the emotional power of her brand story.
She is changing too slowly because enterprise buyers dislike speed.
questions.explanation: The old tactics may still contain useful pieces, but they cannot lead until the enterprise terrain is read. The issue is stale command from past success, not brand emotion.

questions.prompt: A school principal faces a new phone policy debate and immediately reaches for the discipline plan that solved hallway fights five years ago. Which first move fits present-tense reading?
choices: Announce the old discipline plan quickly to show consistency.
List what is materially different about phones, enforcement, parents, and classroom use before choosing a method.
Discard every prior discipline practice because technology makes the issue entirely new.
questions.explanation: The principal needs to inspect changed conditions before choosing. Reusing the old plan may miss the new terrain, while discarding all prior practice falls into novelty worship.

questions.prompt: A restaurant group expands from one beloved dining room into airport kiosks. The owner wants the same long table-service script. Which choice best avoids fighting the last war?
choices: Use the same script because it created the brand reputation.
Replace the whole brand identity with generic airport convenience language.
Keep the food promise, but redesign ordering, packaging, and staffing for travelers with ten minutes.
questions.explanation: The stable promise can stay, but the airport context changes time, flow, and buyer need. The right answer keeps earned experience after current constraints reorder it.

questions.prompt: A sales director says, 'This market looks like 2019, so we should repeat the 2019 discount campaign.' A colleague pushes back by asking about buyer budgets, approval cycles, and competitor pricing. What is the colleague doing?
choices: Practicing present-tense reading before memory chooses the tactic.
Undermining a proven strategy without evidence.
Overvaluing novelty because the calendar year is different.
questions.explanation: The colleague is testing resemblance against current conditions. The old campaign might still work, but only after budgets, approval cycles, and pricing show the terrain is truly similar.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit throws out its donor-calling process because the new campaign uses text messages, then donations fall. The donors still wanted personal recognition. What mistake did the team make?
choices: They failed to automate the text messages fast enough.
They ignored the novelty reversal and discarded a stable human need.
They should have kept every old script word for word.
questions.explanation: Not every new channel changes the underlying job. The team mistook new technology for a new donor psychology and threw away a practice that still fit.

questions.prompt: A coach's team moves to a league with larger fields and stricter referees. Last year's aggressive pressure worked on smaller fields. Which plan is strongest?
choices: Keep the full pressure system because changing would weaken identity.
Abandon pressure entirely because the league label changed.
Teach selective pressure triggers and recovery shape after mapping the new field and referee conditions.
questions.explanation: Selective triggers let the coach keep useful experience while adapting to real changes. Keeping everything or abandoning everything both let memory or novelty decide too early.

questions.prompt: A cybersecurity lead sees a breach that resembles last quarter's phishing incident, but the logs show device-prompt approvals after phone calls with internal project details. What should she infer?
choices: The resemblance is useful, but the actual method demands a revised response.
The old phishing checklist should be run unchanged because resemblance is enough.
The incident is completely unrelated to phishing and no old steps apply.
questions.explanation: Surface similarity should start investigation, not end it. Some containment steps may transfer, but the live method points to verification and device-approval controls.

questions.prompt: A publisher's print subscription drive once won on a free tote bag and renewal postcard. In a paid app launch, which first question best protects against the last-war reflex?
choices: Which old tactic can we copy fastest?
What does the current reader believe they are paying for now?
How do we make the app feel as different as possible?
questions.explanation: The reader's current purchase logic should lead. Copying speed repeats the old war, while forcing difference for its own sake confuses novelty with judgment.

questions.prompt: A product team debates whether to reuse a playbook from a successful consumer launch for a regulated medical customer. Which evaluation is best?
choices: Reject the playbook entirely because regulation makes every prior lesson useless.
Use the playbook exactly because success is the strongest evidence available.
Compare buyer, risk, approval path, and evidence needs before deciding which pieces survive.
questions.explanation: The evaluation tests old tools against current terrain. It avoids automatic repetition and avoids the opposite error of treating a new label as proof that nothing transfers.

reviewCards.front: A tactic once made you successful. What must happen before you use it in a changed situation?
reviewCards.back: Read the present terrain first: incentives, rules, timing, risks, buyer, and power. Past success becomes useful evidence only after you test which conditions still match.

reviewCards.front: A new label makes everyone want to discard the old process. What check prevents novelty worship?
reviewCards.back: Ask what actually changed and what stayed stable. If the channel or vocabulary changed but the underlying need did not, preserve the useful old practice and adjust only the evidence or delivery.

reviewCards.front: Your team says, 'We have seen this before.' What question should follow immediately?
reviewCards.back: Ask, 'Which live conditions prove that?' Resemblance is only a starting clue. The current rules, incentives, and risks must confirm whether the old playbook still fits.

reviewCards.front: A breach looks like the previous incident, but one log detail does not fit. What should you do?
reviewCards.back: Treat the old checklist as partial. Use the mismatch to update the response, because the detail that does not fit may be the part that reveals the real terrain.

reviewCards.front: What is the danger of success in this strategy?
reviewCards.back: Success makes repetition feel like wisdom. The better habit is to let past wins advise after the present has been inspected, not before.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to make experience answer to current facts. The skill is not forgetting the past; it is stopping the past from choosing before the present has been read.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a team says an old tactic worked before, then list the current buyer, rule, risk, and timing differences before approving it.
If a problem sounds new, then identify which underlying need or constraint may still be old before you discard prior tools.
If a checklist feels familiar, then look for the one fact that does not fit before you run the checklist unchanged.
If you are using the style that won your last role, then ask what your current role rewards that the last one did not.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one plan you are about to reuse. Write two columns: changed conditions and stable conditions. Remove or revise one tactic that appears only in the wrong column.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, choose one active project and ask where memory may be issuing orders. Note one old tool to keep, one to revise, and one to retire because the terrain has changed.

memorableLines.text: Memory is trying to run the meeting.
memorableLines.why: It turns the last-war reflex into a visible pressure inside the room.

memorableLines.text: The live terrain gets the first vote.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the chapter's mental move into one plain rule.
It gives the reader a short command that resists both stale habit and novelty chasing.
